definition: to sing, chant; 1. intransitive: to sing to the praise of any one, Eph. 5:19; Col. 3:16 (in both passages of the lyrical emotion of a devout and grateful soul). 2. transitive: to sing a song, Rev. 5:9.

another, other; a. absolutely: Matt. 27:42; 20:3; Mark 6:15; Acts 19:32; 21:34, and often. b. as an adjective: Matt. 2:12; 4:21; John 14:16; 1 Cor. 10:29. c. with the article: the other (of two), Matt. 5:39; 12:13; the others, all others, the remainder, the rest: John 21:8; 1 Cor. 14:29. [Synonyms: allos as compared with heteros denotes numerical in distinction from qualitative difference.]
Amphipolis, the metropolis of Macedonia Prima; so called because the Strymon flowed around it (Thucydides 4, 102); formerly called "Nine Ways" (Thucydides 1, 100): Acts 17:1.

Artemis, that is to say, the so-called Tauric or Persian or Ephesian Artemis, the goddess of many Asiatic peoples, to be distinguished from the Artemis of the Greeks, the sister of Apollo [Bible Dictionary s.v. Diana]. A very splendid temple was built to her at Ephesus, which was set on fire by Herostratus and reduced to ashes, but afterwards, in the time of Alexander the Great, rebuilt (Acts 19). [Excerpt.]

reflexive pronoun of the third person (himself, herself, itself; plural themselves). It is used 1. of the third person singular and plural, to denote that the agent and the person acted on are the same: to save himself, Matt. 27:42; Mark 15:31; Luke 23:35; to humble himself, Matt. 23:12. It is also often added to middle verbs, John 19:24.
Enos (i.e. man, mortal), son of Seth (Gen. 4:26): Luke 3:38.

the other; another, other. It refers 1. to number, as opposed to some former person or thing; a. without the article, other: joined to a noun denoting some number or class within which others are distinguished from the one, Matt. 12:45 and Luke 11:26, seven other spirits, i.e. to be distinguished from the one already mentioned; Mark 16:12; Luke 6:6; 9:56; John 19:37; Acts 2:40; 4:12; Rom. 7:3; 8:39; 13:9; other generations, i.e. past generations, Eph. 3:5.

Euroclydon, the reading of the Received Text at Acts 27:14 for the name of a stormy wind; the critical editions read Euraquilo, a north-east wind (from the Greek euros and the Latin aquilo; Vulgate euroaquilo). Not found elsewhere.

to will, wish; and 1. commonly, to will deliberately, have a purpose, be minded: followed by an infinitive, Mark 15:15; Acts 5:28, 33; 12:4; 15:37; 18:27; 19:30; 2 Cor. 1:15; Heb. 6:17; 2 John 12; 3 John 10; Jude 5; James 1:18 (of his own free will he brought us forth). [Excerpt; Thayer's full article is several columns long.]

1. down, downwards: Matt. 4:6; Luke 4:9; John 8:6, 8; Acts 20:9. 2. below, beneath; a. of place: Mark 14:66; Acts 2:19; to the bottom, Matt. 27:51; Mark 15:38; the parts or regions that lie beneath (opposed to heaven), i.e. the earth, John 8:23. b. of temporal succession: from two years old and under, Matt. 2:16.

properly, to transpose, transfer, remove from one place to another: of change of situation or place, mountains, 1 Cor. 13:2 (Isa. 54:10); into the kingdom, Col. 1:13; to remove from the office of steward, Luke 16:4; to remove from life, Acts 13:22; metaphorically, to lead aside to other tenets, to turn away, Acts 19:26.

(from mēde and heis) it is used either in connection with a noun, none, or absolutely, no one, not one, no man; neuter, nothing; and in the same constructions as mē; accordingly a. with an imperative, the person to whom something is forbidden: 1 Cor. 3:18, 21; 10:24; Gal. 6:17; Eph. 5:6; Col. 2:18; 1 Tim. 4:12; Titus 2:15; James 1:13; 1 John 3:7.

to build a house, erect a building; a. properly, to build (up from the foundation): absolutely, Luke 11:48; 14:30; 17:28; the builders, Matt. 21:42; Mark 12:10; Luke 20:17; 1 Pet. 2:7 (from Ps. 118:22); to build upon a foundation laid by others, i.e. to carry on instruction begun by others, Rom. 15:20; a tower, Matt. 21:33; Mark 12:1; Luke 14:28; barns, Luke 12:18; a temple, Mark 14:58; John 2:20; a house upon a rock, Matt. 7:24, 26; Luke 6:48; contextually, to restore by building, to rebuild, repair: Matt. 23:29; 26:61; 27:40; Mark 15:29; Luke 11:47. b. metaphorically, to found: upon this rock I will build my church, Matt. 16:18. [Excerpt.]

an adverb which denies simply (and thus differs from mēketi), no longer, no more, no further: Matt. 19:6; Mark 10:8; Luke 15:19, 21; John 4:42; 6:66; Acts 20:25, 38; Rom. 6:9; 14:15; 2 Cor. 5:16; Gal. 3:25; 4:7. [Excerpt.]

demonstrative pronoun, this; used I. absolutely: this one, visibly present here: Matt. 3:17; 17:5; Mark 9:7; Luke 7:44; 9:35; 2 Pet. 1:17; Matt. 9:3; 21:38; Mark 14:69; Luke 2:34; 23:2; John 1:15, 30; 7:25; 9:8; 18:21, 30; 21:21; Acts 2:15; 4:10; 9:21. [Excerpt; Thayer's full article is several columns long.]

to owe; a. properly, to owe money, be in debt for: Matt. 18:28; Luke 16:5, 7; 7:41; Philem. 18; that which is due, the debt, Matt. 18:30, 34. b. metaphorically: the good-will due (due benevolence), 1 Cor. 7:3; owe no one anything except to love one another, because we must never cease loving and the debt of love can never be paid, Rom. 13:8; absolutely, to be a debtor, be bound: Matt. 23:16, 18; followed by an infinitive, to be under obligation, bound by duty or necessity, to do something; it behoves one; one ought: Luke 17:10; John 13:14; 19:7 (he ought to die); Acts 17:29; Rom. 15:1, 27; 1 Cor. 5:10. [Excerpt.]
(from para, beside, and legō, to lay) to sail past, coast along: Crete, Acts 27:8, 13. (Vulgate lego, i.e. to sail past, coast along; Latin legere oram.)
(superlative of polus) most: plural, Matt. 11:20; a very great multitude, Mark 4:1; the most part of the multitude, Matt. 21:8; adverbially, at the most, 1 Cor. 14:27.
much speaking (Latin multiloquium): Matt. 6:7. (Prov. 10:19; Xenophon, Plato, Aristotle, Plutarch.)

much; used a. of multitude, number, etc., many, numerous, great: a great number, Acts 11:21; much people, Acts 18:10; a great multitude, Mark 5:24; 6:34; 8:1; Luke 7:11; 8:4; John 6:2, 5; Rev. 7:9; 19:6; Mark 3:7; Luke 5:6; Acts 14:1. [Excerpt; Thayer's full article is several columns long.]
labor, toil; 1. i.q. great trouble, intense desire: on behalf of any one, Col. 4:13. 2. pain: Rev. 16:10, 11; 21:4.
(second aorist of prooraō) to foresee: Acts 2:31; Gal. 3:8.

properly, to put a stumbling-block or impediment in the way, upon which another may trip and fall; to be a stumbling-block; in the N. T. always metaphorically (R. V. to cause or make to stumble; A. V. to offend, cause to offend); a. to entice to sin: Matt. 5:29, 30; 18:6, 8, 9; Mark 9:42, 43, 45, 47; Luke 17:2; 1 Cor. 8:13; passive, to be offended, Rom. 14:21; 2 Cor. 11:29. b. to cause a person to begin to distrust and desert one whom he ought to trust and obey; to cause to fall away, and in the passive to fall away: John 6:61; Matt. 13:21; 24:10; 26:33; Mark 4:17; 14:29; to be offended in one, i.e. to see in another what I disapprove of and what hinders me from acknowledging his authority: Matt. 11:6; 13:57; 26:31; Mark 6:3; 14:27; Luke 7:23. [Excerpt.]

properly, the movable stick or trigger of a trap, trap-stick; a trap, snare; any impediment placed in the way and causing one to stumble or fall, a stumbling-block, occasion of stumbling: Lev. 19:14; a rock of offence, i.e. a rock which is a cause of stumbling, figuratively applied to Jesus Christ, whose person and career were so contrary to the expectations of the Jews concerning the Messiah that they rejected him, Rom. 9:33 and 1 Pet. 2:8 (from Isa. 8:14). b. metaphorically, any person or thing by which one is drawn into error or sin; of persons: Matt. 13:41; 16:23; so Christ crucified is called, 1 Cor. 1:23; of things: to put a stumbling-block in one's way, i.e. to do that by which another is led to sin, Rom. 14:13; Rev. 2:14; 1 John 2:10. [Excerpt.]
1. an observer, a watchman. 2. the distant mark looked at, the goal or end one has in view: toward the goal, Phil. 3:14.

(Latin conscientia; literally 'joint-knowledge'), i.e. a. the consciousness of anything: a soul conscious of sins, Heb. 10:2. b. the soul as distinguishing between what is morally good and bad, prompting to do the former and shun the latter, commending the one, condemning the other; conscience: Rom. 2:15; 9:1; 1 Cor. 8:7, 10, 12; 10:29; Heb. 9:14; one's own conscience, 1 Tim. 4:2; for conscience' sake, because conscience requires it, Rom. 13:5; in order not to occasion scruples of conscience in another, 1 Cor. 10:28; questioning nothing, as though such questioning were demanded by conscience, 1 Cor. 10:25, 27; because conscience is impressed and governed by the idea of God, 1 Pet. 2:19. [Excerpt.]

(also sunistanō, sunistaō) 1. to place together, to set in the same place, to bring or band together; in the intransitive tenses, to stand with or near: Luke 9:32. 2. to set one with another, i.e. by way of presenting or introducing him, i.e. to commend: 2 Cor. 3:1; 6:4; 10:12, 18; Rom. 16:1; 2 Cor. 5:12; 4:2; 12:11. 3. to put together by way of composition or combination, to teach by combining and comparing, hence to show, prove, establish, exhibit: Rom. 3:5; 5:8; 2 Cor. 6:4; Gal. 2:18; 2 Cor. 7:11. 4. to put together, unite parts into one whole; to be composed of, consist: 2 Pet. 3:5; to cohere, hold together: all things consist (hold together) in him, Col. 1:17.

a. properly, held as of great price, i.e. precious: stones, Rev. 17:4; 18:12, 16; 21:19; 1 Cor. 3:12 (R. V. costly stones); comparative, 1 Pet. 1:7; superlative, Rev. 18:12; 21:11. b. metaphorically, held in honor, esteemed, especially dear: Heb. 13:4; to one, Acts 5:34; 20:24. [Excerpt.]
such, generally with an implied suggestion of something excellent or admirable: 2 Pet. 1:17.

such as this, of this kind or sort; a. joined to nouns: Matt. 9:8; 18:5; Mark 4:33; 6:2; 7:8, 13; 9:37; John 9:16; Acts 16:24; 1 Cor. 5:1; 11:16; 2 Cor. 3:4, 12; 12:3; Heb. 7:26; 8:1; 12:3; 13:16; James 4:16. b. correlatively: Mark 13:19; 1 Cor. 15:48; 2 Cor. 10:11; Acts 26:29; Philem. 9. c. used substantively: John 4:23; Luke 9:9; 13:2; with the article, one who is of such a character, such a one: Acts 22:22; 1 Cor. 5:5; plural, Matt. 19:14; Mark 10:14; Luke 18:16; John 8:5; Rom. 16:18; 1 Cor. 7:28; 16:16, 18. [Excerpt.]

present subjunctive of eimi, 'to be' (Thayer treats all forms of the verb under eimi): I. eimi has the force of a predicate (i.e. is the substantive verb): to be, i.e. 1. to exist. [Excerpt from the article on eimi.]
